categories.name: The season
categories.description: What the sea brings, month by month.

categories.name: Suppliers
categories.description: The farmers, brokers and brewers we buy from.

posts.title: The first kohada of autumn
posts.excerpt: Gizzard shad is the fish an Edomae counter is judged by. This week the first good ones came in.
posts.content:
Kohada is a small, silver fish that tastes of almost nothing until it is salted, rinsed and laid in vinegar. Done well, it is the most Edomae piece of the evening.

This week the broker at Kanemasa Fish called at five in the morning: the first fish of the right size had arrived. They are on the counter from tonight, cured for forty minutes, rested for a day.

posts.title: Why our rice is red
posts.excerpt: The pale brown colour of our rice comes from red vinegar made from sake lees. Here is why we use it.
posts.content:
Guests sometimes ask if the rice is brown rice. It is not: it is white Koshihikari seasoned with akazu, a red vinegar made from the lees left after brewing sake.

Akazu is softer and rounder than rice vinegar, and asks for less sugar. It holds up to strong, oily fish, and it is how sushi was seasoned in Edo.

posts.title: Ten days of tuna
posts.excerpt: Fresh is not always best. Why our medium-fat tuna rests in the cold room for up to ten days.
posts.content:
A tuna loin on the day it is cut is firm and a little metallic. Wrapped in cloth and rested at one degree, it softens, and its taste deepens.

We check it twice a day. Some loins are ready after five days, some after ten. The plate legend marks it as Akami, on indigo glaze.

posts.title: A morning at Hoshino Farm
posts.excerpt: Every September Chef Senda visits the terraced field our rice comes from.
posts.content:
The field is small: eleven terraces on a north-facing slope, so the rice ripens slowly. The Hoshino family has farmed it for four generations.

We buy the whole harvest and have it milled weekly, so the rice on the counter is never more than seven days from the husk.

posts.title: Five pours for autumn
posts.excerpt: The new sake pairing follows the plate legend, from hinoki to grey stoneware.
posts.content:
Hiyaoroshi, sake rested through summer and released in autumn, opens the pairing beside the small dishes.

For the tuna we pour a warm junmai from Morikawa Brewery; for the close, a little aged sake, the colour of tea.

posts.title: Green tea at the end
posts.excerpt: Why the last thing on the counter is a tall cup of powdered green tea.
posts.content:
Agari, the tea served at the end of a sushi meal, is strong and plain. It clears the palate after the tamago and tells you, gently, that the evening is over.

In winter we change to a roasted tea, which is softer and warms the hands.
